prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit.

We represent: plaintiff.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that the improper joinder doctrine requires the removing party to show there is no reasonable basis to predict recovery against the in-state defendant.

Cite at least six decisions of the Fifth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**I. The removing defendants must show there is no reasonable basis to predict that Plaintiff could recover against the in-state defendant.**

A defendant may remove a case on diversity grounds only if complete diversity exists and no properly joined defendant is a forum citizen. Under the improper joinder doctrine, a court disregards the citizenship of an in-state defendant if the removing party shows that the defendant was improperly joined. *Smallwood v. Ill. Cent. R.R. Co.*, 385 F.3d 568, 572–73 (5th Cir. 2004) (en banc). The doctrine is a narrow exception to the rule of complete diversity. *Int'l Energy Ventures Mgmt., L.L.C. v. United Energy Grp., Ltd.*, 818 F.3d 193, 200 (5th Cir. 2016). Defendants invoking it carry a heavy burden.

**A. The governing standard places a heavy burden on the removing party.**

A removing party can establish improper joinder in two ways. It can show actual fraud in the pleading of jurisdictional facts. Or it can show that the plaintiff is *unable to establish a cause of action against the non-diverse defendant in state court*. *Travis v. Irby*, 326 F.3d 644, 646–47 (5th Cir. 2003); *Smallwood*, 385 F.3d at 573. Defendants do not allege fraud here, so only the second route is open to them. On that route, the test is "whether the defendant has demonstrated that there is no possibility of recovery by the plaintiff against an in-state defendant, which stated differently means that there is no reasonable basis for the district court to predict that the plaintiff might be able to recover against an in-state defendant." *Smallwood*, 385 F.3d at 573; accord *Campbell v. Stone Ins., Inc.*, 509 F.3d 665, 669 (5th Cir. 2007); *McDonal v. Abbott Labs.*, 408 F.3d 177, 183 (5th Cir. 2005).

The burden of persuasion stays with the removing party throughout. That party must prove improper joinder, and it must do so by more than a showing that recovery is unlikely. *Griggs v. State Farm Lloyds*, 181 F.3d 694, 699–700 (5th Cir. 1999); *Cuevas v. BAC Home Loans Servicing, LP*, 648 F.3d 242, 249 (5th Cir. 2011). The standard also requires more than a theoretical possibility of recovery. The question is whether there is a reasonable basis to predict that state law might impose liability on the facts involved. *Campbell*, 509 F.3d at 669. Any doubt about the propriety of removal is resolved in favor of remand. *Cuevas*, 648 F.3d at 249.

**B. The court resolves the inquiry in the plaintiff's favor.**

The court ordinarily resolves the question by conducting a Rule 12(b)(6)-type analysis of the complaint. It asks whether the complaint states a claim against the in-state defendant under state law. *Smallwood*, 385 F.3d at 573; *Int'l Energy Ventures*, 818 F.3d at 200. The court also resolves all disputed questions of fact and all ambiguities in controlling state law in the plaintiff's favor. *Burden v. Gen. Dynamics Corp.*, 60 F.3d 213, 216 (5th Cir. 1995); *Great Plains Trust Co. v. Morgan Stanley Dean Witter & Co.*, 313 F.3d 305, 312 (5th Cir. 2002). The court does not decide whether the plaintiff will actually or even probably prevail on the merits. It looks only for a possibility of recovery. *Davidson v. Ga.-Pac., L.L.C.*, 819 F.3d 758, 765 (5th Cir. 2016). If that possibility exists, the in-state defendant was properly joined, and the case must be remanded. *Smallwood*, 385 F.3d at 573.

A court may "pierce the pleadings" only in a narrow set of cases. In those cases the plaintiff has misstated or omitted discrete facts that would determine whether joinder is proper. Even then, the court's inquiry is limited. It may not use the summary inquiry to pre-try the merits. *Smallwood*, 385 F.3d at 573–74; *Davidson*, 819 F.3d at 765.

**C. Application.**

Plaintiff's complaint alleges specific facts against the in-state defendant. Those facts state a claim under the governing state law. Defendants therefore must show that state law forecloses any recovery on those facts. They have not done so. At most they dispute the merits of Plaintiff's claim, and that dispute does not support a finding of improper joinder. Because Defendants have not carried their heavy burden, the in-state defendant was properly joined. Complete diversity is lacking, and the Court should remand.
